title: Testing FastAPI endpoints

spans.text: WHY USE THIS?
Testing FastAPI endpoints checks status codes, response data, and error cases without connecting to a live network or database.
PURPOSE AND REAL-WORLD USE

FastAPI's `TestClient` calls endpoints without starting a live server. Tests check status codes, JSON bodies, and error behavior; keep them repeatable and independent of the external network. Install with `pip install fastapi httpx`.

To run these examples locally, install `pip install fastapi uvicorn httpx` plus any extra package named in the lesson. Save the server example as `app.py` and start `uvicorn app:app --reload`. `--reload` is for development only.

WHERE DOES THIS APPEAR IN REAL LIFE?
A shop test checks item creation, 404 for a missing item, and rejection of an invalid body.
If this part is omitted: Without tests, a change can break a working endpoint and the first report may come from a user.

REQUEST AND EXPECTED RESPONSE

spans.code:
Request: TestClient GET /ping → status 200 və {"message":"pong"}
Response: `GET /ping` returns 200 and `{"message":"pong"}`; the script prints `route test passed`.

spans.text:
LINE-BY-LINE CODE EXPLANATION
`from fastapi import FastAPI` — Imports FastAPI so the program can create its application object; without it, `FastAPI` is undefined.
`from fastapi.testclient import TestClient` — Imports TestClient so an HTTP request can exercise the app without opening a server port.
`app = FastAPI()` — `FastAPI()` creates the ASGI application that holds the routes and is passed to the server.
`@app.get("/ping")` — Binds an HTTP method and URL path to this function; without the decorator, it is not an API endpoint.
`def ping():` — Defines the endpoint the server calls; parameter names help bind path, query, or body data.
`return {"message": "pong"}` — Returns the HTTP response value; FastAPI converts it to JSON and applies the response model.
`client = TestClient(app)` — Runs work for this request; its result or side effect affects the response.
`response = client.get("/ping")` — Sends the stated GET request through the test client and stores the response.
`assert response.status_code == 200` — Continues the application's data handling or control flow.
`assert response.json() == {"message": "pong"}` — Runs work for this request; its result or side effect affects the response.
`print("route test passed")` — Runs work for this request; its result or side effect affects the response.
PRACTICE: CHECK IT WITH AN HTTP CLIENT
This complete file calls the app locally with TestClient; it does not open a server port. Install `httpx` for TestClient.
COMPLETE RUNNABLE CLIENT TEST
QUESTION: What will this code print? Predict first, then run it.

spans.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/ping")
def ping():
    return {"message": "pong"}

client = TestClient(app)
response = client.get("/ping")
assert response.status_code == 200
assert response.json() == {"message": "pong"}
print("route test passed")

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

with TestClient(app) as client:
    response = client.get("/ping")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    print(response.json())

COMMON MISTAKES
Checking only `response.json()`; also assert the status, error response, and input boundaries.

spans.title: Practical tip
spans.text: Reset application state per test; use an isolated test database and dependency override when testing database routes.

spans.title: One level deeper
spans.text: `TestClient` lets synchronous tests exercise HTTP behavior; replacing external services with fakes keeps tests fast and reliable.

spans.title: Important warning
spans.text: Tests should not use real user data or a production database; use isolated state that can be reset.
QUICK RECALL
Question: Which action best prevents the common mistake from this lesson?
Answer: Reset application state per test; use an isolated test database and dependency override when testing database routes.
